svg.aria-label: How pixels leave the chip and how the panel lights them up. The upper half is inside the silicon: the display controller's video port emits twenty-four parallel data wires plus three synchronisation wires, one pixel per clock; the MIPI DSI controller packs each line of pixels into a packet with error checking; and the D-PHY serialises those packets onto four differential data lanes plus one clock lane. Those lanes are drawn as byte streams to make the point that what travels on the flex cable is a serial bit stream, not addresses and not pixels in parallel. Below a marked boundary is the panel itself, a separate component on the far end of the flex cable. Inside it a display driver integrated circuit receives the packets and converts them back to parallel: a source driver with three thousand two hundred and forty outputs drives one whole row of subpixels at once along the columns, while a gate driver with two thousand four hundred outputs selects one row at a time, and the pixel array sits at the intersection. A single line runs backwards from the driver chip to the system on chip, the tearing effect signal, which is the only backwards-travelling line in the whole figure: it is the panel telling the chip that it has just finished a refresh and that it is now safe to send the next frame. The closing note is that the signal changes form three times on this journey, parallel to serial and back to parallel, but it is never stored along the way
svg.font-family: Poppins, 'Noto Sans SC', 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif
svg.text: OUT OF THE CHIP AND INTO THE GLASS
this is the one place in the whole path where the signal actually changes form.
parallel inside the chip → serial on the cable → parallel again inside the panel. stored nowhere along the way.
adds ECC and checksum per packet
source driver · 3240 outputs · one whole row at once
the source driver holds one row of colours; the gate driver picks which row gets it. 2400 rows, 60 times a second.
the only line in this figure that runs backwards is the one the panel uses to say “I have just finished a refresh”.
that line is the tearing effect signal, turned on with the DCS command SET_TEAR_ON, 0x35 (include/video/mipi_display.h:115,
issued at drm_mipi_dsi.c:1380). without it a command-mode panel has no way to know when writing is safe. lane count is not fixed by
the standard — each panel declares its own (include/drm/drm_mipi_dsi.h:192), and four is simply what a 1080p 60 Hz phone needs.
